name: Change Blindness
description: People are strikingly poor at detecting even large changes to a scene when the moment of change itself is masked (e.g. by a blink, cut, or blank flash), because attention, not raw visual exposure, is what makes a change perceptible from one glance to the next.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to interface transitions and live-updating dashboards: a state change that isn't paired with an attention cue (motion, highlight, animation) risks going unnoticed even when it's visually large.
prevalence_note: Recognized in interaction-design and dashboard/data-viz discourse specifically (justifying animated transitions on state change), though not as universally cited outside that niche as e.g. anchoring or scarcity.

findings.description: When a brief blank field masks the motion transient between an original and a modified scene, observers become strikingly poor at detecting even large, repeated changes; detection is much faster when a verbal cue names the changed object or when the changed object is of high semantic interest in the scene — evidence that attention, not raw visibility, gates change perception, and that people do not hold a complete detailed representation of a scene from one glance to the next.
findings.source_title: To See or Not to See: The Need for Attention to Perceive Changes in Scenes
